correctness.rationale: The affine interpolant takes the signed values 1/u, 1/v and -1/(u+v) at u², v² and (u+v)². These are all three roots of z q(z)^2-1, whose leading coefficient is their inverse product. Under the two spectral-anchor hypothesis, any SPD preconditioned matrix of condition 1 must be I, and its only additional distinct eigenvalue of A is thus (u+v)². The threshold ((u+v)/u)^2>4 is strict, with every larger value attained and dimension 3 minimal. Left Arnoldi on B=I returns q(A)b; it attains relative error 2 on the third mode, despite exact evaluation of the preconditioned action. For the full-support pilot, moment orthogonality gives the stated increasing Ritz trace s1 and determinant s0; s1+sqrt(s0) increases from 7 and crosses 9 once, with the sign restriction 9-s1>0 at the positive quadratic root. In fact q_t(1) and q_t(4) stay positive throughout. At the crossing B_t is singular and there is no Arnoldi initialization on b=e3. Away from the crossing the one-mode output is sign(q_t(9))e3/3. At t=0 the first derivatives of the three preconditioned eigenvalues are -400/27, 400/27 and -400/3, giving the claimed quotient expansion for small positive t. The pilot g_t and application b are separate as specified. Independent bounded symbolic and numerical reproduction (`python3 independent_check.py`) rechecked these identities and the leading slope; the original checker was inspected, not executed. Exact arithmetic and the scoped two-node interpolation class are essential.

value.rationale: It shows exactly when perfect squared preconditioning fails to certify the target branch in a basic interpolation model, and that even full-support two-step pilots do not remove the issue: the method can give 200% error with conditioning tending to one. The sharp boundary is useful for separating a condition-number certificate from a branch certificate. The pilot construction complements the exact identity example without purporting to measure generic error rates or the performance of globally positive polynomials.
